title: WORD OF MOUTH ISN'T A MARKETING PLAN
text: The referral still happens the old way. Your customer tells her neighbor about the deck, the neighbor takes your name, and then she does exactly what you'd do: pulls out her phone. 91% of homeowners still find their pros through word-of-mouth. Almost none of them call before checking you out online first. The referral gets you into the research. It no longer skips it. That's the shift a lot of owners haven't priced in. "All my work comes from referrals" used to be a marketing plan. Now it's a pipeline with an invisible leak: names recommended at barbecues, then quietly dropped after a ninety-second phone search you never see. What Happens in Those Ninety Seconds She types your business name. What loads decides the call. A Google profile with a real star rating, recent reviews, photos of actual local work, and calm answers to the people who complained: that's a green light. A half-claimed listing with nine reviews, the newest from two years ago and one angry one sitting unanswered: that's a name off the list, and nobody tells you it happened. The numbers here are blunt. 81% of homeowners lean on Google reviews to decide on a business. 41% now always read reviews before making contact, up from 29% just a year earlier. And 88% say they'd pick a business that responds to all of its reviews. They aren't reading your five-star raves for entertainment. They're reading how you answered the one-star. A referral doesn't close the job anymore. It nominates you for a background check you didn't know was running. Where the Leak Shows Up You won't see it directly, but you'll see the symptoms. Referred quotes that used to close at eight in ten now close at five. The customer who says "I'd heard about you but couldn't find much." The competitor whose work you'd redo for free winning your side of the street on the strength of 300 reviews. An electrician with twenty years of flawless panels can lose, sight unseen, to a two-truck outfit with a photo habit. The record beats the reputation that never got written down. The Front Door Is Moving Again The second shift is faster. A year ago, about 6% of consumers used AI tools to find or vet local businesses. It's now 45%. When someone asks an assistant for a good plumber nearby, the answer gets assembled from the same public record: your reviews, your profile, your photos, the text on your site. There's no ad to buy inside that answer. The businesses that surface are the ones with the deepest, freshest proof, which means the work you do to convert referrals is the same work that gets you recommended to strangers. The Minimum Viable Presence You don't need to become a marketer. You need a proof habit. Five moves, none of them over fifteen minutes: Claim and complete your Google Business Profile. Every field: services, hours, service area, license info. A complete profile outranks a thin one and reads as legitimate to a stranger deciding at a red light. The three-photo habit. Before, during, after, on every job. A roofer with 200 photos of real local roofs doesn't need copywriting. The pictures are the pitch. The driveway ask. The moment the customer says it looks great is the moment to ask. Text the direct review link from the truck before you pull away. Asked-for reviews land at several times the rate of hoped-for ones. Answer everything. Two sentences on the good ones. On the bad one: calm, factual, offering to make it right. You're writing for the hundred future readers, not the one reviewer. A one-page site that loads on a phone. Who you are, what you do, where you work, photos, a number that gets answered. She's reading it in her driveway. Speed beats design. The ask, scripted Keep it human: "Reviews are how a shop our size competes with the big guys. If you've got two minutes, it genuinely matters to us." Send the direct link, not instructions. One polite follow-up a week later, then let it go. That ritual alone, run on every happy customer for a season, rebuilds most thin profiles. Three Checks to Run Tonight Grab your phone, open a private browser tab, and search your business name plus your town. First: what actually loads. Is the profile yours, is it complete, and are the photos recent, or is the newest proof of your work older than your newest truck? Second: the gap. Pull up the competitor who keeps winning bids around you and compare review count, recency, and whether they answer people. That delta is the leak, measured. Third: tap your own website on cell data, not shop Wi-Fi. If it takes longer to load than a customer waits at a red light, it's costing you calls. Twenty minutes, three checks, and you'll know exactly which of the five moves to start with. Reputation Compounds. Referrals Don't. A referral is earned once and spent once. The public record works every night, for every searcher, including the ones no neighbor ever talks to. And it pays a premium: 72% of homeowners say they'd pay up to 10% more for the pro with the stronger service reputation. That's the quiet math of the whole thing. The crew that photographs its work and answers its reviews isn't doing marketing instead of craftsmanship. It's making the craftsmanship admissible as evidence. Word of mouth still starts every good thing in this business. Just stop letting it end there.
